1 # gcec rules 2 3 The project's standing working rules — injected at session start while this pack 4 is declared. Activity-scoped procedures live in this pack's skills 5 (snapshot-approval, merge-and-ci, testing-guide) and surface on 6 demand; the extractor-automation domain's standing rules are the "Extractor 7 pipeline" section below, and its scheduled tasks live under `tasks/`. 8 9 ## Working rules 10 11 - **A duplicate dispatch-trigger arriving while a session's own delegated 12 subagent is still running is a signal to stop, not to investigate.** 13 Confirm it via `resolve-dispatch` (the "not mine, change nothing" case) and 14 end the turn — don't let that check snowball into re-reading the subagent's 15 targets and redoing its work. In #876 a dispatched `tidy-issues` subagent 16 was still running in the background when a duplicate webhook fired; the 17 top-level session's "just confirming" pass over all 16 target issues 18 escalated into closing one and posting reconfirmation comments on the 19 rest — duplicating, not verifying, work its own subagent was already 20 producing — and converged the dispatch issue on that duplicate instead of 21 the subagent's actual output. (duplicate-dispatch-trigger) 22 - **`get_job_logs`'s `tail_lines` can blow the tool's token limit on its own** 23 (canon covers capping and qualifying list/search calls) — guessing a large 24 value to diagnose a CI failure can itself exceed the limit (#1101, 25 `tail_lines: 2406` → `exceeds maximum allowed tokens`). Skip the guess — a 26 small call gets you the saved-to-disk log path, then `grep` that file for the 27 failure marker (`not ok`, `FAIL`) the same way an oversized list/search 28 result gets read. (getjoblogss-taillines-can) 29 - **This repo's one divergence from the canon merge recipe: CI must be green 30 first** — twice for e2e/heavy-browser changes. The project mechanics of driving 31 a merge (dispatching CI in a web session, the poll back-off, when to arm 32 auto-merge instead of waiting) are the merge-and-ci skill — **load it for any PR a session opens**, including one 33 opened incidentally mid-task by an unattended run, not only for a deliberate 34 merge. (repos-divergence-canon) 35 - **`npm run regen` is the regenerator** (load lists + UI snapshots + 36 generic-coverage baseline/report); a stale artifact can't slip through — its 37 own gate fails. On the `ours` driver (kept in sync with `.gitattributes`): 38 `extension/event-extractors/load-order.generated.json` (from `npm run index`), 39 `dev/requirements//cases/*.png` (from `npm run refresh:ui`), and 40 `dev/requirements/extractor/generic-coverage/generic-coverage.baseline.GENERATED.json` 41 (npm-run-regen) 42 + `generic-coverage.GENERATED.md` (from the generic-coverage test). The 43 inline gallery in `dev/requirements/requirements.md` is part-authored prose — 44 **not** on the `ours` driver; reconcile via `npm run regen` + the gallery 45 drift gate. If `regen` reports a coverage regression, that's the real gate 46 firing — review it, don't paper over it. 47 - **Keep divergence small**: when syncing a branch to `origin/main` (by rebase), 48 **run `npm run regen`** as part of the sync, so the branch carries 49 freshly-generated artifacts, not just the latest sources. (keep-divergence-small) 50 51 ## Owner commands 52 53 - **"bump version"** = cut a release **end to end** — bump, merge, and wait for 54 the published artifact. The bump mechanics are the canon `bump-version` 55 skill's; honor an explicit target ("bump version to 1.4.0") or level ("bump 56 patch" / "bump major") when given. Open the PR, 57 get CI green, squash-merge with `(#N)` — 58 saying "bump version" is itself the merge authorization for **this** 59 deterministic bump PR only. The merge triggers **Release: Create Package**; 60 do **not** report done until the `vX.Y.Z` GitHub Release with its refreshed 61 `google-calendar-event-creator.zip` asset is published — poll via the GitHub 62 MCP tools on the merge-and-ci skill's back-off. (bump-version) 63 - **"learned lessons"** = run the canon lessons-learned pass over the current 64 conversation on **the strongest model available**. Capture routing: see below. (learned-lessons) 65 66 ## Testing invariants 67 68 - **Integration cases are the reviewed contract** — a person reads 69 `dev/requirements/extractor/expected/`; nobody reviews the unit tests. Every 70 required change or bugfix gets a case (one real, focused page per distinct 71 behavior; keep cases minimal). Unit tests under `extension-test/` are a 72 supplementary safety net for page-independent logic. (integration-cases-reviewed) 73 - **`extension-test/` mirrors `extension/`'s tree, one test per source file** 74 (`extension//.js` → `extension-test//.test.js`). 75 Deliberate departures: `extension-test/integration/` for 76 whole-extension/interaction tests; no mirror for `custom/*` sources or 77 data/markup files (covered by live cases / snapshots / drift guards); 78 `extension-test/harness.js` is shared infra (not a test) and stays at the 79 root. (extension-test-mirrors) 80 - **The pinned `REFERENCE_NOW`** (`dev/requirements/shared/reference-time.js`, 81 currently 2026-06-01) **is the floor of the cases' dates**: author a 82 neutral/upcoming case **on or after it** so it's pill-free; use a past date or 83 a future year only when the case is *pinning* a pill. (pinned-referencenow) 84 85 ## Codebase gotchas 86 87 Project-wide footguns only. Portable rules these instantiate live in the canon 88 packs/skills. 89 90 - **`declarativeContent`/`UrlFilter` host-match verification is CI-only** — the 91 real URL→icon match runs inside Chrome, exercised here only by the CI-only 92 real-Chrome test (`dev/requirements/heavy/extension-load.chrome.test.js`). 93 (declarativecontent-urlfilter-host) 94 - **CDP-introspecting the MV3 worker hits the portable traps** (canon): here 95 they bit `declarativeContent…getRules` (hung until job timeout), which is why 96 the worker publishes `globalThis.iconRulesReady` for the test to poll. (cdp-introspecting-mv3) 97 - **The jsdom-vs-Chrome DOM traps bit this repo directly** (canon): #130/#137 98 drove the **production** remedy the canon (framed for tests) leaves out — 99 strip `noscript`/`script`/`style` from a clone before reading any element's 100 user-facing text (the generic extractor's footer-address reader does this, #675). 101 (jsdom-chrome-dom) 102 - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it** — the parser 103 auto-closes the `

` and the content lands as its `nextElementSibling`; a 104 `.foo p` selector reads `""` with no error. Bit tel-aviv's description blocks 105 (#602) — read the sibling, not the tag. (injected-block-markup) 106 - **The augment-not-replace + reset-per-load rule lands on `GCal` here** 107 (canon): `registry.js` resets `GCal.sources` on load and is pinned **first** 108 in the load order so it runs before any source pushes (#48, #189). (augment-replace-reset) 109 - **`clean()` collapses all whitespace including newlines — single-line fields 110 only.** A description run through it loses every line break (#131, #140, 111 #141); multi-line text goes through the block helpers (`blockText` / 112 `normalizeBlock` / `htmlToText`). Line-break handling is generic, never a 113 per-source choice. (clean-collapses-all) 114 - **A supported/registered host is necessary but not sufficient for "an 115 event"** — gating on `Boolean(site)` surfaced phantom events on home pages 116 (#133); a real event requires actual data (JSON-LD or a parsed date), never a 117 mere host match. (supported-registered-host) 118 119 ## Workflow-failure classification 120 121 **Mind the one gap `gha/scheduled-failure-escalation` can't see:** it only 122 inspects workflows carrying a `schedule:`, so a workflow that is unattended by 123 some *other* trigger — `workflow_run`, `repository_dispatch` — needs its failure 124 job wired by hand. 125 The `Release` stub (`chrome-extension-release.yml`) is exactly that shape; its 126 reporters live in the vendored create-package/publish/daily workflows it calls. 127 128 ## Extractor pipeline 129 130 Standing rules for the extractor-automation domain — the two gcec pack 131 [`tasks/`](tasks/): **create-extractor** (an `extractor-request` issue → a PR 132 adding site support, and the sweep that records a committed `.url`'s missing 133 cached page) and the weekly **generic-extractor-improvements** (read a spec only when working 134 on that pipeline). Adding or refreshing a cached live case by hand is the 135 [testing-guide](skills/testing-guide/SKILL.md) skill. 136 137 - **All page fetching goes through [`scraperapi.mjs`](tasks/create-extractor/scraperapi.mjs), from a 138 task's preprocessing worker and nowhere else.** A rendered fetch through 139 ScraperAPI's residential proxy (`render=true`, so a single-page app records 140 post-render HTML with real data). Bot-blocking from CI/sandbox IPs is the 141 portable rule maintained in the canon; here the escape hatch is the 142 `SCRAPER_API_KEY` **GitHub Actions secret**, named in both tasks' 143 `required_secrets` — never a local fetch (this sandbox is bot-blocked), and 144 never an agent session. ScraperAPI is the whole fetching surface — swap the 145 vendor in that one module if it underperforms. The aid for a flaky SPA render is 146 the **`Wait-for selector`** a source request can carry 147 (`extension/events-popup/derive-wait-selector.js`, a source-request tool, NOT an 148 event extractor, #603), passed through as `wait_for_selector`. (all-page-fetching) 149 - **Facebook can't be a cached live case** — a hard HTTP 400 even through the 150 proxy, so its extraction stays unit-tests-only 151 (`extension-test/event-extractors/extraction.test.js`). (facebook-cant-be) 152 - **A scratch script that needs a project dependency (e.g. `jsdom`) can't live 153 in the harness's external scratchpad** — Node's module resolution walks up 154 from the script's own directory, which never reaches this repo's 155 `node_modules`. `generic-extractor-improvements`' habitual "fetch a page, 156 then jsdom-inspect it" throwaway scripts need to live inside the repo (a 157 gitignored scratch dir, cleaned up before committing) instead (#866). (scratch-script-needs) 158 - **Rendered output isn't deterministic.** A re-record can legitimately shift a 159 live case's `expected` — treat such drift like a site-markup change, and prefer 160 extracting JSON-LD/`og:` (which apps still inject) over brittle DOM positions. 161 (rendered-output-isnt) 162 - **An ambiguous numeric slash date is read by the page's declared locale, 163 centrally — never per-source, never guessed.** `"05/07/2026"` (both parts ≤ 12) 164 reads month-first by default (V8's US convention) and flips day-first only on a 165 *positive* non-US signal — an explicit non-US region in `` / 166 `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` (region unknown) stays 167 month-first rather than guess. 1	import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
2	import { join } from 'node:path';
3	import { finding } from './findings.mjs';
4	import { parseYaml } from './minimal-yaml.mjs';
5	import { stripComments } from './code-scanning.mjs';
6	import { normalizeEdges, barrierFindings, staleFindings } from './reference-scanning.mjs';
7	
8	// The declarative pattern-check engine: a rule whose whole logic is "these
9	// patterns over these files" is DECLARED as data — and data is JSON, not code.
10	// A pack's declarations live in `packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json` (a skill's
11	// in `<pack>/skills/<name>/declared-checks.json`), an array of specs the pack
12	// registry discovers structurally and compiles here into ordinary
13	// `{ id, severity, why, run(ctx) }` rule objects the runner treats like any
14	// other. Nothing wires them: dropping a declaration into the file adds it.
15	//
16	// The format admits no comments — the pattern plus its failureMessage/what/fix
17	// text IS the check — and no prose pointers: a declaration states its own case
18	// or it isn't finished. So a spec carries exactly:
19	//   id              the rule id settings and findings name it by
20	//   severity        'blocking' | 'advisory'
21	//   since           optional 'YYYY-MM-DD' — the date this check was added. A
22	//                   blocking check is enforced as advisory for its first
23	//                   GRACE_DAYS from it (helpers/findings.mjs), so a check can
24	//                   land against a tree that still violates it.
25	//   failureMessage  why this matters, printed on every finding the rule makes
26	//   …the assertions below, each with the `what` and `fix` it fails with
27	//
28	// REGEXES ARE STRINGS in `/body/flags` form — "/^\\s*schedule:/m" — compiled at
29	// load. Keys that accept a path instead (scanFiles, excludeFiles, pathExists)
30	// read any other string as an exact repo path; at every other pattern key a
31	// string that is not in `/…/` form is an authoring error, reported as one.
32	// The engine owns only the walking (the mechanism/policy line line-scanning.mjs
33	// draws): every pattern, file filter, and failure text stays in the declaration.
34	// Spec keys are deliberately wordy — a declaration must read as the whole check
35	// without this header.
36	//
37	// Built for MANY such rules at once: however many pattern rules a run holds,
38	// the engine makes ONE pass over the scanned tree — each file is read once and
39	// its lines split once, with every subscribing rule's assertions evaluated in
40	// that single visit — and the per-context results are cached, so the first
41	// pattern rule the runner reaches pays for the whole family and the rest are
42	// lookups. Regexes must be non-global (`.test` on a /g regex is stateful).
43	//
44	// A key the vocabulary cannot place is DROPPED at load, not thrown on: it is a
45	// typo (asserting nothing, silently) or a key a newer engine knows, and the load
46	// cannot tell them apart. Refusing it would wedge the second case — a member's
47	// pack lane and engine lane converge on separate cycles, so a declaration can
48	// legitimately reach an engine older than its vocabulary, and the converge that
49	// would deliver the newer engine is itself gated on the load (#1400). The typo is
50	// caught instead by the `declared-check-spec-keys` world rule, advisory where the
51	// skew is possible and blocking in the canon, where engine and declarations ship
52	// from one commit. A key the engine DOES place keeps its loud failure on a broken
53	// value (an uncompilable regex, a malformed date): that is not skew, it is broken.
54	//
55	// The spec vocabulary — everything beyond the rule metadata is optional:
56	//   fix                rule-level default: any assertion declaring `what` but
57	//                      no `fix` of its own inherits this one (for rules whose
58	//                      every assertion shares one remedy)
59	//   scope              "work" = this declaration judges the CHANGE rather than
60	//                      the repo, so it runs in check_the_work and may carry the
61	//                      work assertions below. Absent = world scope, the default
62	//                      (the pack manifest's own two rule lists say the same
63	//                      thing for a coded rule — a declaration has no list to
64	//                      sit in, so it states its scope here)
65	//   scanFiles          which files the content assertions read, in one of three
66	//                      forms: a RegExp over repo paths, one exact path (read
67	//                      directly), or an object naming the files ANOTHER parsed
68	//                      document points at —
69	//                        { inParsedFilesMatching, whereFileContains,
70	//                          namedByField, defaultingTo, withSuffix }
71	//                      every tracked document `inParsedFilesMatching` (refined
72	//                      by the `whereFileContains` probe) is parsed, the string
73	//                      at `namedByField` read from it — an array anywhere along

180	//                      that must not exist under a layout ({path} interpolates);
181	//                      excludeFiles applies
182	//   extractValueSets   [{ setName, whenSetEmpty, and exactly one source:
183	//                         fromParsedFile | fromParsedFilesMatching

191	//                      requireIndexCoverage's eachValueOfSet) assert over. A
192	//                      parsed source reads the string values of the arrays at

207	//                      groups of the path and line regexes that found it, and
208	//                      all of them interpolate into the quantifiers' templates

210	//                      file is one value at its first origin. whenSetEmpty is
211	//                      declared, never defaulted: "assertNothing" makes every
212	//                      consumer of an empty set assert nothing, { what, fix }
213	//                      reports the empty set itself at its source — two
214	//                      different verdicts (prose naming no knobs; an audit

216	//   checkSetValues     [{ setName, valueIsPattern, and exactly one of
217	//                         requireSomeFileMatching: { pathMatching, text },
218	//                         forbidEveryFileMatching: { pathMatching, text },
219	//                         requirePathExists, requireTrackedPathMatching,
220	//                         what, fix }]
221	//                      pass TWO: for every value of the named set, some
222	//                      in-scope file whose path matches the filled pathMatching
223	//                      must have text matching the filled `text` / no such file
224	//                      may / the filled path must exist / some tracked path must
225	//                      match the filled pattern. Every pattern here is a
226	//                      TEMPLATE in /body/flags form: {value}, {path}, {line} and

229	//                      valueIsPattern, which inserts {value} raw because the

233	//                      anchors at the

264	//                      by the first-token glob of some non-comment index line

266	//                      only), or by the parsed index's array at `atField`

270	//                      whenIndexFileAbsent = "assertNothing" | "flagEveryPath",

274	// The structured-data assertions read PARSED documents — `.json` via JSON.parse,
275	// `.yaml`/`.yml` via the minimal YAML parser — each file parsed at most once per
276	// scan, shared by every rule; an absent or unparsable document asserts nothing.
277	// A field path is dot-separated (`devDependencies.esbuild`), and a field counts
278	// as present when its value is not undefined:
279	//   checkParsedFiles   [{ file | filesMatching (+ whereFileContains)
280	//                         | everyScannedFile: true,
281	//                         forEachEntryAtField, whereEntryFieldEquals:
282	//                           { field, equals },
283	//                         whenFieldPresent,
284	//                         requireField, requireFieldMatching: { field, pattern },
285	//                         forbidField,
286	//                         forbidValueInArray | requireValueInArray:
287	//                           { atField, value, ignoreCase,
288	//                             matchingEntryObjectsByField },
289	//                         requireEqualFields: { field, inFile, atField,
290	//                           whenFileMissing, whenUnequal },
291	//                         what, fix }]
292	//                      the select-then-assert family: pick documents (one
293	//                      exact `file`, every tracked file `filesMatching` whose
294	//                      text matches `whereFileContains`, or whatever the rule's
295	//                      own `scanFiles` selected — `everyScannedFile`, the way a
296	//                      field-named scan set is asserted over), optionally
297	//                      quantify over the named entries of the object at
298	//                      `forEachEntryAtField` (kept where `whereEntryFieldEquals`
299	//                      holds; {entry} interpolates), gate on `whenFieldPresent`,
300	//                      then assert: `requireField` present / the value at
301	//                      `requireFieldMatching.field` matching its `pattern` as
302	//                      text (so a field present but blank still fails) /
303	//                      `forbidField`
304	//                      absent / the array at `forbidValueInArray.atField` free
305	//                      of the value, or holding it under `requireValueInArray`
306	//                      (either way an entry that is an object counts by its
307	//                      `matchingEntryObjectsByField` field; a missing or
308	//                      non-array field satisfies forbid and fails require) /
309	//                      the base's `field` equal to `inFile`'s `atField` (an
310	//                      absent `inFile` fires `whenFileMissing` at its path; a
311	//                      mismatch fires `whenUnequal` with {first}/{second})
312	//   checkKeyValueFile  [{ file, keys, whenMissing, whenLineNotKeyValue,
313	//                         whenKeyUnknown, whenKeyMissing }]
314	//                      the dotenv-style file must exist, hold only KEY=value
315	//                      lines and # comments, use only the declared keys, and
316	//                      declare every one; {key}/{keys}/{line} interpolate
317	//
318	// The WORK assertions — declarable only under `scope: "work"`, and reading the
319	// change rather than the tree: the branch's commit messages, the merges it
320	// introduces, and each file's parsed base beside its parsed head (work.mjs owns
321	// those surfaces). They run per rule, outside the shared file scan:
322	//   checkBranchCommits [{ someMessageMatches, unlessOnDefaultBranch, what, fix }]
323	//                      one finding at "(branch)" when NO commit message since
324	//                      the base matches; a branch carrying no commits of its
325	//                      own asserts nothing, and unlessOnDefaultBranch exempts
326	//                      main/master. {commits} (the count) and {base} interpolate
327	//   forbidIntroducedMergeCommits { what, fix }
328	//                      one finding per merge commit the change introduces —
329	//                      merges already on the base are the repo's history, not
330	//                      the work — anchored at "<branch>@<sha>"; {sha} and
331	//                      {subject} interpolate
332	//   forbidAddedValueInArray [{ file | filesMatching (+ whereFileContains),
333	//                              atFields, what, fix }]
334	//                      one finding per value the change ADDS to any of the JSON
335	//                      arrays at `atFields`, comparing the parsed head against
336	//                      the parsed base — a set comparison, never the text diff,
337	//                      because appending an array element re-touches the line
338	//                      above it. An unparsable head asserts nothing; an absent
339	//                      base makes every value an addition. {value} interpolates
340	//   forbidAddedLinesMatching [{ inFilesMatching, match, unlessLineMatches, what, fix }]
341	//                      one finding per line the change ADDS (in a changed file
342	//                      the path pattern selects) that `match` hits and
343	//                      `unlessLineMatches` does not; a brand-new file's every
344	//                      line is added. {match} interpolates
345	//   forbidRemovedLinesMatching [{ inFilesMatching, match, unlessLineMatches,
346	//                                 unlessMatchRemainsInFile, what, fix }]
347	//                      the mirror: one finding per line the change REMOVES,
348	//                      anchored where the base held it — an append-only file's
349	//                      rule. unlessMatchRemainsInFile: true forgives a removal
350	//                      whose matched text the file still carries somewhere (a
351	//                      reworded line is a removal plus an addition to the
352	//                      diff, not a loss). {match} interpolates
353	//   requireCoChange    [{ whenChangedFileMatches | whenAddedLineMatches:
354	//                           { inFilesMatching, match },
355	//                         requireChangedFileMatching, what, fix }]
356	//                      a change to one thing requires a change to another in
357	//                      the same branch: where some changed file matches the
358	//                      first pattern (or some added line in such a file matches
359	//                      the second), some changed file must match
360	//                      `requireChangedFileMatching`; one finding per triggering
361	//                      file when none does ({path} = that file)
362	//   flagUntrackedFilesMatching [{ match, what, fix }]
363	//                      one finding per file in the run's set that git does not
364	//                      track — the test a `git ls-files`-driven suite never ran
365	//   whenReplyClassIncludes  a class name, or a list of them — "correction",
366	//                      "feature", "process-change", "other": a RULE-LEVEL gate
367	//                      on the session's declared comment classes (the
368	//                      classification lines the replies carry), so a work rule
369	//                      can say "on a process change, the diff must reach the
370	//                      local packs". Every assertion of the rule asserts
371	//                      nothing unless some reply declared one of the classes;
372	//                      no transcript, nothing asserted

374	// The ACTION assertion — declarable only under `scope: "action"`: a rule about
375	// a TOOL CALL, evaluated twice from one declaration. The PreToolUse hook

# Changing a pack's elements

A pack's carriers - the rules in `RULES.md`, a skill and its triggers, a coded or declared
check, a task and its policy, the manifest - say *what* a session does. The decision behind
each - why it reads so, who decided, from what evidence, why this carrier and this trigger,
what was rejected, what would retire it - is one append-only file per element under the
pack's `provenance/`, read by maintenance and never by a session. Three things follow for
any edit under a pack.

## 1. The edit owes an entry, in the same change

Every change to what a carrier decides lands with an entry on the element's file, and the
`provenance-change-recorded` check says so again at the Stop hook when it did not. Which
file: the marker that ends a rule or guideline names it (`(url-filter-host-operators)` →
`provenance/url-filter-host-operators.md`), and two carriers may name one file while their
history is one; an unmarked guideline's is its skill's; a skill's is its directory name; a
check's its id with `/` as `-`; a task's its id; the manifest's `_pack.md`. Which kind:

| The change | Kind |
|---|---|
| a rule, guideline, skill body or step reads differently | `reworded` - or `strengthened` / `weakened` when the modality moved |
| a rule split in two, or two folded into one | `split` / `merged` (an entry on every file involved) |
| a guideline given a file of its own, its history having diverged from its skill's | `split` on the skill's file, `born` on the bullet's, with `Mechanism` |
| a rule moved to another carrier or pack | `moved`, with `Mechanism` |
| prose turned into a check | `converted`, with `Mechanism` and the deletion-test verdict |
| a skill's description or `force-load-on-*` trigger | `trigger-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a task's preconditions, `expected_outcome`, `automerge`, model or worker | `policy-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a check's severity, or the gate deciding when it fires | `severity-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| what an element applies to, where its text reads the same - a manifest's `requires` or fingerprint, a check's file scope, a skill's corpus | `scope-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a new element | `born`, with `Mechanism` - and `mark` first if the carrier has no file |
| an element removed | `retired` - the file stays, and this is its last entry |
| a review that found new evidence or changed the retire test | `reaffirmed`; a review that found nothing new writes nothing |

No entry is owed for whitespace, a re-wrap, a code comment in a check, a fixture, a test, a
README row, a version bump, or the marking pass's own markers and `body:` lines.

Write the entry in the file grammar and append it through the tool, which validates it and
refuses one that carries a secret:

```
node packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs append <pack> <element> <<'EOF'
## 2026-09-21 · reworded · the consequence clause said why twice (#2210)
- **Reason:** the second sentence restated the rule; cut.
- **Actor:** @handle (owner).
- **Model:** <the model this session runs, as the harness names it>
- **Landed:** #2210
EOF
```

In a member the tool is `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs`, and
the pack is under `.claudinite/local/packs/`. `--changed` in place of the element appends the
same entry to every element the working tree's diff touched - a sweep's one-line entries.
The fields, each written only where there is something behind it: `Source`, `Reason`,
`Actor` (the person by handle with their role, or the run and who merged it - never an
email), `Model`, `Mechanism` (the carrier and its trigger, and why - required on `born`,
`converted`, `moved`, `trigger-changed`, `policy-changed`, `severity-changed`), `Rejected`,
`Retire when`, `Landed`. An entry never restates the rule: the carrier is the description,
the entry is the decision. A candidate turned down goes on `_declined.md` the same way, kind
`declined`, with `Source`, `Reason` and `Actor`.

**Size the entry to the decision, never to the work.** Most are three to five lines. Each
field is the shortest answer that is still an answer, and one clause is usually the whole of
one - `Reason: the folder never existed.` Where a required `Mechanism` keeps the carrier it
already had, the new value is the whole of it - `a regex` - and the why-clause is owed only
where the choice of carrier was itself the decision. The diff, the commit message and the
pull request already hold what changed, how it was proved and what it cost; an entry
retelling any of them writes the record twice and buries the line a review came for. Length
is earned only by a decision that was weighed - an alternative turned down, a constraint that
forced the shape - so a corrected path, a repointed pattern or a renamed field gets one line,
and a change nobody deliberated over gets `Reason` alone. Cut a field rather than pad it, and
cut one that repeats another field or the entry's own title.

A file is meant to grow: a wrong entry is answered by a later one, never by editing the one
that was wrong. The check advises against a line lost or altered and refuses nothing.

### The one lane that writes the past

`append` and `apply` are append-only, and the tool enforces it: an entry dated before the
file's last is refused, because a change being recorded now cannot have happened before the
change recorded last. **The backfill is the deliberate exception**, and `--backfill` on
either command is how it says so. It is deriving a history that already happened, so its
entries are dated in the past by definition, and under that flag the file is re-rendered in
date order rather than appended to. Two things only it may do:

- **Replace what the references conversion wrote.** A file the conversion filled carries a
  `born` dated by the conversion write rather than by the element. Where the derived birth
  is earlier, that placeholder is what is being corrected and the tool drops it, naming it
  in the run's output; where the placeholder's date *is* the birth, no earlier born arrives
  and it stands. The dates decide, so neither truncating these files as a class nor leaving
  them is the rule. Only the conversion's own entry is ever replaced - an entry somebody
  wrote is never dropped, whatever its date.
- **Open a file the marking pass could not.** An element retired *before* that pass is named
  by no carrier, so nothing will ever create its file. A `--backfill` batch that opens with
  `born` creates it; its whole history, birth through `retired`, arrives at once or not at
  all. Do not put such a history on `_pack.md` instead: a `retired` entry seals the file it
  ends, and `_pack.md` is the one file in a pack that must stay appendable forever.

Every other caller - every change being made now - uses the plain lane, where a file only
ever grows at its end.

## 2. The README carries use, never history

A pack's `README.md` is for the person adopting the pack or reaching for one of its
elements: when the pack activates, what each check demands and what satisfies it, when a
skill is the thing to load, what the task does to the repository, and the catalog of what
the pack carries. Never how an element came to be, what it replaced, why its id reads as it
does, what an earlier shape did, or how the pack is maintained. The test is the sentence: a
date, a pull request number, an "until", a "was", a "kept as it was" or a "distilled from"
is a decision, and a decision is an entry on the element's file - `_pack.md` for the pack's
own shape. Move it there; do not write it here.

## 3. The mount is never edited

A file under `.claudinite/shared/` arrived from a canon and the next converge replaces the
whole tree. Change it in the canon, or carry the difference in the repo's own
`.claudinite/local/packs/`.

# Writing pack prose

Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.

**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.

## The ration

Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.

- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
  trigger.
- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs on the element's
  provenance file (below).
- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads.
- **Starting a `SKILL.md`, or editing one that declares no body** — say under its frontmatter
  `metadata` what the body is: `body: workflow` for a procedure, whose steps and their gotchas
  change as one, or `body: guidelines` for rules behind a trigger, kept on the skill's one file
  until one has a history of its own. A skill that mixes the two declares the shape of its
  greater part. The harness ignores the key; the corpus's own maintenance reads it, and never
  infers it.

## Shape a rule so it fires

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it.
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets.
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change.
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it.
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command.
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
  reader doesn't need at act time goes on the element's provenance file (below).
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find.
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.

## The provenance log - where a rule's rationale lives

A pack keeps one file per element under `provenance/`, beside its `RULES.md`: an append-only
log of the decisions behind the element, read by maintenance and review - the pass that asks
whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written - and never by a session.
No rule sends its reader there, nothing loads it, and it never vendors: a member mounting a
canon pack receives the rules, not the reasoning behind them. The grammar, the kinds, the
fields and the tool are [changing-pack-elements](../changing-pack-elements/SKILL.md)'s; what
this skill adds is how a rule is written so the log can hold it.

- **Ending a rule** - every rule in a `RULES.md` ends with the bare marker naming its file -
  `… never a filesystem walk. (url-filter-host-operators)` - and nothing else: don't name the
  folder, don't link it, don't ask the reader to follow anything. The marker is the element's
  id: two to four hyphenated words for the guideline rather than its wording, chosen once and
  never renamed, so a rewording never touches it and a member's override can name it. Two
  rules whose history is one may share a marker. A guidelines skill's bullets are the skill's
  file's and carry none, until one's history diverges and it takes a marker and a file of its
  own; a workflow skill's steps carry none, the skill being the element.
- **Adding a rule** - write the brief rule and end it with its marker; create its file with a
  `born` entry through `provenance.mjs append` (`mark` creates the file where none exists),
  and put the reason there, never in the rule. A consequence the reader needs under pressure
  earns its clause; rationale the reader doesn't need at act time is the entry's. Write the
  entry so a future review can **reaffirm the rule from it** - `Retire when` is what would
  have to be true for the rule to go.
  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    the error, the measured cost).
  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it - in a member's
    local pack; a canon file carries the paraphrase, never the quote.
- **Rewording, moving, splitting or converting a rule** - the entry is owed in the same
  change, and the forced skill names its kind.
- **A check's rationale** - on the check's own file, named by its id (`cer/version-bumped` →
  `cer-version-bumped.md`); nothing is added to the check.
- **Removing a rule or check** - its file stays and gains a `retired` entry as its last, in
  the same change.

The `provenance-integrity` check holds the mechanism together - every carrier names a live
file, every file parses - and `provenance-change-recorded` holds the change: a carrier that
changed lands with its entry. A pack not yet on the convention is put there by
`provenance.mjs mark`, and its history filled by the
[backfilling-provenance](../backfilling-provenance/SKILL.md) skill; nothing here is done rule by
rule.

## Evidence

The commit and its PR remain the archive - the story of the incident, quoted exchanges and
session ids live there and in the capture, never in the rule and never in a canon's log. What
an entry takes from them is only the **reaffirmable core**: `Source` and `Reason`, the minimum
a future review needs to re-test the rule, and `Retire when`, the test it is reaffirmed
against. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument - a cost
the reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Naming the thing a fixture stands for** - invent the name (`acme-pack`, `acme-user`,
  `acme.example`) wherever the case holds for any name at all, and keep a real one only where that
  entity is what the case asserts about: a borrowed name reads as meaningful, collides with the
  real thing's own cases, and makes every later rename an edit of tests that were never about it.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- **Asserting on a record the code under test produced** — a finding, a parsed spec, a normalized declaration — assert the fields that code **computed**, and leave the ones it copied straight through from its own declaration or from your setup. A check selected by its id whose test then reads `finding.rule` back, or restates the `severity` its declaration set, is asserting the selector: it stays green however wrong the matching is, and goes red only when someone deliberately renames or re-grades the rule. One computed field identifies a record — the rest is your setup talking back to you.
- **A coupling that must hold for every member of a set** — each task's id matching the directory it is discovered by, each check's `doc:` pointer resolving, each declaration validating — assert it once in a sweep that reads the whole set out of the tree, never in each member's own suite. The per-member copy only ever holds the members that happen to have a suite, so it under-covers and taxes at the same time: the shape is billed to each suite that has one while the members without one go unguarded.
- **Pinning the text a finding or error carries** — assert the part the code **derived** from the input (the version it tells you to bump to, the path it resolved, the term it names), and leave the static sentence alone. A remedy's wording is prose someone will improve, and asserted back it turns every rewording into a test edit while guarding nothing — those words were read straight out of the declaration the test already points at.
- **Sweeping a set** — a tree walk, a filter over a file's lines, a loop over discovered
  members — **pin how many members it covered**, beside the loop. An assertion reached only
  inside a loop, or only behind an `if`, says nothing about the members that never entered it,
  so a set that quietly shrinks — a renamed token, a moved directory, one call kind of two
  dropping out — leaves the survivors passing and reports that pass for the whole. A count read
  off the same source is the pin (`assert.ok(files.length >= 25)`), and a guard *inside* the
  loop needs its own, since the
  outer count says nothing about how many members reached the assertion behind it.
- **Reading the source *text* of a module the test could `import`** — asserting an identifier
  appears in it, or that one string precedes another in the file — inverts the signal: it goes
  red on a pure rename and stays green on a behaviour change that leaves the tokens in place.
  Grepping a *different* artifact is the two-artifact drift guard above and stays. Where the
  module is callable and a grep is still the only way in, report that its entry point does the
  whole job at once — that is worth more than the assertion.
- **Choosing the cases for a validator, parser or guard** — its own rejection branches are the
  list: for each, write the input that forces it. A branch nothing forces is either a promise
  no test holds or one the code can no longer reach, and both are worth finding. The gap
  clusters on the **present-but-unusable** input — the empty string, the directory that will
  not read, the module that throws on import — because absent and valid are the two cases
  everyone writes, while the field that is there and broken is the one that arrives in
  production.
- **A comparison against a threshold, a deadline or an anchor instant** — test the value
  exactly **on** it, not only either side. `<=` and `<` differ on exactly one input, so a suite
  that samples comfortably around the boundary agrees with both and pins neither. Where a cron
  or a poll drives the comparison, that one input is the ordinary case rather than the edge: the
  run fires *at* the anchor.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism.
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- **A shared fixture helper is paid for by every test that calls it**, so build the part that is identical for every case — a scratch repo's `init` and seed commit, a migrated database, a compiled bundle — once per process and copy it, rather than rebuilding it per test.

- **A test runner parallelises across FILES, so one file's serial runtime is a floor no worker count clears.** When a suite's CPU sits well below its core count, the idle cores are waiting on that file — give it intra-file concurrency, which more workers cannot substitute for.

- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically.
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

entries.name: mcp__github__add_issue_comment
entries.description: Add a comment and/or reaction to a specific issue or issue comment in a GitHub repository. Use this tool with pull requests as well (in this case pass pull request number as issue_number), but only if user is not asking specifically to add or react to review comments. At least one of body or reaction is required.

body.description: Comment content. Required unless reaction is provided.

comment_id.description: The numeric ID of the issue or pull request comment to react to. Use this for reactions to comments; omit it to react to the issue or pull request itself. Cannot be combined with body.

issue_number.description: Issue or pull request number to comment on or react to.

reaction.description: Emoji reaction to add. Required unless body is provided.

entries.name: mcp__github__issue_write
entries.description: Create a new or update an existing issue in a GitHub repository.

assignees.description: Usernames to assign to this issue

duplicate_of.description: Issue number that this issue is a duplicate of. Required when state_reason is 'duplicate'.

delete.description: Set to true to clear this field's current value on the issue. When false or omitted, this property is ignored. Cannot be true when 'value' or 'field_option_name' is provided.

field_name.description: Issue field name (case-insensitive). Must match a field returned by list_issue_fields for this repository or its organization.

field_option_name.description: Option name for single-select fields. Validated against the field's options before the API call. Cannot be combined with 'value' or 'delete: true'.

value.description: Value to set. Use for text, number, and date fields (date as YYYY-MM-DD). For single-select fields, prefer 'field_option_name' so the option is validated before the API call. Cannot be combined with 'field_option_name' or 'delete: true'.

issue_fields.description: Issue field values to set or clear. Each item requires 'field_name' and exactly one of 'value', 'field_option_name', or 'delete: true'.

labels.description: Labels to apply to this issue

method.description:
Write operation to perform on a single issue.
Options are:
- 'create' - creates a new issue.
- 'update' - updates an existing issue.

parent_issue_number.description: Issue number of the parent issue. Only used when method is 'create' and cannot be combined with issue_fields. The new issue is created and attached to this parent in the same operation.

parent_owner.description: Repository owner of the parent issue. Must be provided with parent_repo. Omit both to use owner and repo. Only used when method is 'create' and parent_issue_number is provided.

parent_repo.description: Repository name of the parent issue. Must be provided with parent_owner. Omit both to use owner and repo. Only used when method is 'create' and parent_issue_number is provided.

state_reason.description: Reason for the state change. Ignored unless state is changed.

type.description: Type of this issue. For updates, pass null to remove the current type. Only use if issue types are enabled for this repository. Use list_issue_types to get valid type values for this repository or its owner organization. If the repository doesn't support issue types, omit this parameter.
